channel.title: Said & Checked: Rhode Island — AskAmerica
channel.description: What officeholders said each day from or about Rhode Island, and which statements government data supports, contradicts or rules out.

item.title: Said & Checked, Rhode Island, 2026-11-21: none false or contradicted, 1 unsettled (Sheldon Whitehouse)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “We actually have standing to enforce” Unsettled. The Congressional Record confirms the remark, and the introduced text of S. 5653 read on govinfo.gov contains no provision found that gives senators or Congress standing to enforce understandings with the Defense or Interior Departments; the engrossed text that passed was not read. Whether senators would have standing turns on how courts apply standing doctrine and on what 'standing' the speaker meant, which the bill text does not decide.

item.title: Said & Checked, Rhode Island, 2026-11-20: none false or contradicted, 1 unsupported, 3 unsettled (Sheldon Whitehouse)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsupported and Unsettled

  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “in Rhode Island, the NEPA environmental review process was estimated to add thousands of dollars to the cost of each replacement bus shelter.” Unsupported. No source documenting a per-shelter NEPA cost in Rhode Island was found; the search covered the warehouse catalog, web searches and ecoRI's reporting on RIPTA shelters, and RIPTA's board packet refused the fetch.
  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “Reported as: Whitehouse also said the bill would make data centers pay for the power they use.” Unsettled. S. 5653 as introduced adds a Federal Power Act section 228 that bars shifting the incremental grid costs of data centers drawing 20 megawatts or more to other customers and requires recovery from the data center; it addresses grid costs they cause rather than power use in general. The Capito substitute that the Senate actually passed as H.R. 2347 on Nov. 19 could not be read, so whether the provision survived is unconfirmed.
  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “Rather than wait 5 or 10 years to get a bridge or tunnel permitted, BAAJA will reduce those timelines to a little over 2 years.” Unsettled. The bill sets a 2-year deadline for environmental impact statements, but CEQ's January 2025 report puts the median recent statement at 2.2 to 2.8 years, with a quarter taking more than six years, and existing law already sets a 2-year deadline, so the 5-to-10-year premise fits only slower cases.
